item.title: “Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be. See the world with its multitude,…
item.description:
“Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be.

See the world with its multitude,
Overcome by ignorance,
Beings given to birth,
Delighting in becoming,
Not freed from existence.

For one who burns up existence,
At all times and places,
All this existence —
Impermanent, suffering, subject to change —

Seeing this as it really is
With perfect wisdom,
Craving for existence is abandoned,
As is the delight in non-existence.

With the complete destruction of craving,
Dispassion, cessation, complete,
That is Nibbāna.
That monk, cooled,
Without clinging to renewed existence,
Has conquered Māra,
Won the battle,
Crossed over all forms of existence.”

From: Udana 3.10
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?” “Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual…
item.description:
“Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?”
“Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual desire, are synonymous with what is called ‘stain.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 5 – Anaṅgaṇasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments,…
item.description:
“Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments, sometimes, from time to time, distorted thoughts, thoughts and considerations connected with attachments continue to arise. Udāyi, mindfulness arises slowly and he quickly abandons that thought, dispels it, ends it, destroys it. Udāyi, just as a man might drop two or three drops of water onto an iron pan that has been heated all day—slowly those drops fall, quickly they evaporate and vanish. Udāyi, I say: ‘This person is still bound, not freed.’ Why is that? Udāyi, the difference in his faculties has been fully understood by me.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 66 – Laṭukikopamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does…
item.description:
“And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … Lord of gods, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. This, lord of gods, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now attain Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.118
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, friend, does one guard the sense faculties? Here, friend, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the…
item.description:
“And how, friend, does one guard the sense faculties? Here, friend, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the eye, practices restraint of the eye. When he hears a sound with the ear … smells an odor with the nose … tastes a flavor with the tongue … feels a touch with the body … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the mind, practices restraint of the mind. Thus, friend, is the guarding of the sense faculties.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.120
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Where the mind is restrained, There suffering ends. If the mind is fully restrained, One is fully freed from suffering. (The Blessed One): One should…
item.description:
Where the mind is restrained,
There suffering ends.
If the mind is fully restrained,
One is fully freed from suffering.

(The Blessed One):
One should not restrain the mind
Completely in every way.
Do not restrain the mind
When self-control is attained.
Where evil states arise,
There one should restrain the mind.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.24
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it.…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it. Looking, reflecting, examining, the foam would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a pile of foam? So too, monks, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — a monk sees form, reflects, examines it. Seeing, reflecting, examining, form appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as…
item.description:
“Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form. If I were to delight in future form, then in the future I would be overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form.’ Reflecting thus, he has no regret for past form, no delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.79
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated,…
item.description:
“That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated, do not fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward others. But many are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, become infatuated, intoxicated, fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward others.

Bemused by wealth and sensual pleasures,
People are greedy and deluded,
In the midst of sensual pleasures,
Without clear awareness,
They are overly intoxicated,
Like a deer unaware of the trap set —
Later they suffer,
Experiencing the results of evil deeds.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell…
item.description:
“Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.” - “Koṭṭhita, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Koṭṭhita, is suffering? The eye is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Forms are suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-consciousness is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-contact is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.163
📖 Read this sutta
